text.p: The following are the main stories from Monday morning's Austrian newspapers.
DER STANDARD
- As many as 20,000 government jobs could be transferred to the private sector, Finance Minister Viktor Klima says.

- The Social Democratic president of Austria's parliament, Heinz Fischer, says Franz Vranitzky should remain federal chancellor despite suffering stinging losses in European Parliament elections two weeks ago.
- Austrians should have more courage to embrace reforms, President Thomas Klestil says in his National Day address.
- Finance Minister Klima says the budget for 1996 and 1997 will be on plan even without several billion schillings in expected revenue from the sale of Creditanstalt.
- Austria's overcrowded banking sector makes for "relatively inefficient" banks, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell says in a study.
- Austrian shares expected to move sideways to lower this week, analysts say.
DIE PRESSE
- Two-thirds of Austrians are against the reform of the German grammar system, a telephone poll shows.
- Danube National Park, covering 9,300 hectares of marshes east of Vienna, officially opened over the weekend.

- Social Democrats have to find their own course, even if that would put them on collision course with the their junior coalition partner, conservative People's Party, vice party leader Heinz Fischer says.
- Trade unions accept the need for deep job cuts among Austria's 70,000 bank employees.
- Two-year austerity budget, a mix of higher taxes and spending cuts, has raised federal government revenues by 41 billion schillings in the first nine months alone, Finance Minister Klima says.
- Turnover in Austria's ailing tourism industry fell by 4.5 percent and overnight stays by 6.2 percent during the summer.
- Investment house Merill Lynch rates VA Stahl as a "buy".
KURIER
- Hannes Swoboda, Social Democrat's top European Parliament candidate, says Chancellor Franz Vranitzky should step down and make room for Finance Minister Viktor Klima in 1997.
- Austria's monopoly postal system needs to cut at least 6,000 of its 54,000 employees.
- Salvage teams find parts of a Slovak tug boat that sank in the Danube last week. River traffic is back to normal.
- European Union to cut down on agricultural subsidies next year. The move should result 500 million schillings in extra transfers to Austria.
SALZBURGER NACHRICHTEN
- Number of overnight tourist stays in Austria over the year looks set to fall below the number recorded in 1970.
- National grid company Verbund reports nine-month pre-tax profit up 7.4 percent.
